newsitem.title: KENYA: COFFEE - Kenya estates urge switch to new variety.
newsitem.headline: COFFEE - Kenya estates urge switch to new variety.

text.p: Kenya's large coffee growers are calling for a switch to a new disease-resistant high-yielding variety in what they see as a revolution for the industry.
Large growers said it was time to sacrifice premiums paid on Kenya's top quality coffees for high yields and lower costs guaranteed by the locally-developed Ruiru 11 coffee variety.
In a coffee development report, they said conversion of existing planted area from traditional varieties to Ruiru 11 would increase cash for the farmer and make the sub-sector more competitive.
The report marks a major policy turnround by large farmers, who previously led a campaign opposed to growing Ruiru 11.

Debate in the industry focussed on the quality aspect of Ruiru 11 which does not have the traditional acidity which attracts the premium prices enjoyed by Kenya, said the report obtained by Reuters on Tuesday.

"However, the plantation sector has forwarded pure Ruiru 11 coffee for sale over the last two years and prices realised have been comparable if not better than for traditional varieties," added the report, written by leading plantations manager Standard Chartered Estate Management Ltd.

"Kenyan coffee growers should look critically at the real margin on the premium price. They should consider foregoing the premium-fetching varieties and replacing them with high yielding varieties like Ruiru 11 or Catimor, which require significantly lower inputs," the report said.
"We know this will sound like a revolutionary concept in the industry which appears tightly tied to conservative tradition.

But reform would benefit the grower and the national economy, it added. The report said actual premiums fecthed by traditional Kenyan coffees had averaged 10 to 15 percent since Kenyan independence from Britain in 1963.

It said direct benefits to growers from a change to Ruiru 11 from traditional varieties such as SL 28 and SL 32 included cutting imput costs by 30 percent, mainly because fungicide spraying would not be necessary because of Ruiru 11's resistance to both coffee berry disease (CBD) and leaf rust.

"It (Ruiru 11) requires very little pruning especially with a four-five year conversion cycle for six-by-eight foot spacing," the report added. "Yield performance is increased by approximately 30 percent."
It gave field production costs for traditional coffee varieties at $853 per tonne versus $569 per tonne for Ruiru 11.
The report said a national effort to rehabilitate the smallholder sector by replanting with Ruiru 11 would require financial support, probably from international donors.
Traders from Japan and the United States have previously said Ruiru 11 was of inferior quality and had a metallic taste.
Just about 5.0 percent of Kenya's total coffee production, estimated at around 95,000 tonnes in 1995/96, is of Ruiru 11.
Kenya has 161,000 hectares of land under coffee. --Nairobi Newsroom ++254-2 330-261
